## Overview

Field experiments are conducted on heterogeneous soil. Neighbouring
plots tend to have similar yields due to shared soil, moisture, and
microclimate conditions. Spatial models account for this correlation,
improving the precision of treatment comparisons.

This tutorial demonstrates how to:

- Visualise spatial patterns in raw data
- Fit first-order autoregressive models: AR1(row) and AR1(row):AR1(col)
- Fit IID spatial random effects as an alternative
- Interpret autoregressive parameters
- Compare spatial residuals before and after correction
- Compute empirical variograms
- Produce publication-quality field heatmaps
- Compare adjusted vs unadjusted BLUPs

The dataset is `agridat::gilmour.serpentine`, a wheat trial on a
22-row by 15-column field with serpentine harvesting pattern.


## Mathematical background

### The spatial mixed model

$$
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{u} + \boldsymbol{\xi} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ is the spatially correlated error and
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is the independent (nugget) error.

### AR1 correlation structure

The first-order autoregressive process defines correlation between
positions $i$ and $j$ as:

$$
\text{Cor}(\xi_i, \xi_j) = \rho^{|i-j|}
$$

where $\rho \in (-1, 1)$ is the autocorrelation parameter. Higher
$|\rho|$ means stronger spatial dependence.

### Separable AR1 x AR1

For a two-dimensional field (rows and columns), the separable model
uses:

$$
\mathbf{R} = \sigma_\xi^2 \left(\mathbf{R}_{\text{row}} \otimes \mathbf{R}_{\text{col}}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{R}_{\text{row}}$ has elements $\rho_r^{|i-i'|}$ and
$\mathbf{R}_{\text{col}}$ has elements $\rho_c^{|j-j'|}$. This is the
standard ASReml spatial model.

### IID spatial random effects

When the AR1 structure is not appropriate (e.g., irregular layouts or
when row/column indices do not reflect spatial proximity), a simpler
approach is to include row, column, or row-by-column interaction as
IID random effects. This absorbs spatial variation without imposing
a specific correlation structure.


## Setup

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library(bayesreml)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(agridat)
```

```{r data}
data(gilmour.serpentine, package = "agridat")
str(gilmour.serpentine)

serp <- gilmour.serpentine
serp$row <- factor(serp$row)
serp$col <- factor(serp$col)
serp$gen <- factor(serp$gen)

# Numeric coordinates for variograms
serp$row_num <- as.numeric(serp$row)
serp$col_num <- as.numeric(serp$col)

cat("Rows:", nlevels(serp$row), "\n")
cat("Columns:", nlevels(serp$col), "\n")
cat("Genotypes:", nlevels(serp$gen), "\n")
cat("Observations:", nrow(serp), "\n")
```


## Exploratory spatial analysis

### Raw data heatmap

```{r raw-heatmap, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
ggplot(serp, aes(x = as.numeric(col), y = as.numeric(row),
                  fill = yield)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "grey90") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "Yield") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(
    x     = "Column",
    y     = "Row",
    title = "Raw yield across the field"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title  = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    panel.grid  = element_blank()
  ) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1)
```

**Interpretation:** Look for gradients (e.g., yield increasing from one
side to the other) or patches (localised high/low areas). These spatial
patterns inflate the error variance if ignored, reducing the power to
detect genotype differences.


### Row and column means

```{r row-col-means, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
row_means <- serp %>%
  group_by(row) %>%
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(yield, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

col_means <- serp %>%
  group_by(col) %>%
  summarise(mean_yield = mean(yield, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

p_row <- ggplot(row_means, aes(x = as.numeric(row), y = mean_yield)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Row", y = "Mean yield", title = "Row means") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))

p_col <- ggplot(col_means, aes(x = as.numeric(col), y = mean_yield)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_point(colour = "#D55E00", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Mean yield", title = "Column means") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))

library(patchwork)
p_row + p_col
```


## Baseline model (no spatial correction)

For comparison, first fit a model without spatial effects:

```{r m-base}
m_base <- bayesreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ 1,
  random    = ~ gen,
  data      = serp,
  n_samples = 1000,
  warmup    = 500,
  chains    = 4
)

summary(m_base)
```


## Model 5a: AR1 in rows only

Model spatial correlation along rows (e.g., within the planting
direction):

$$
\mathbf{R}_{\text{row}} = \sigma_\xi^2 \begin{pmatrix}
1 & \rho_r & \rho_r^2 & \cdots \\
\rho_r & 1 & \rho_r & \cdots \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

In `bayesreml`, the AR1 structure is specified in the residual (rcov)
formula using `ar1()` syntax:

```{r m5a-fit}
m_5a <- bayesreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ 1,
  random    = ~ gen,
  rcov      = ~ ar1(row):id(col),
  data      = serp,
  n_samples = 1000,
  warmup    = 500,
  chains    = 4
)

summary(m_5a)
```

### AR1 parameter interpretation

```{r m5a-ar1-param}
# Extract the autocorrelation parameter
all_draws <- do.call(rbind, lapply(m_5a$greta$draws, as.matrix))
rho_cols <- grep("rho|ar1", colnames(all_draws), value = TRUE)

if (length(rho_cols) > 0) {
  rho_row <- all_draws[, rho_cols[1]]
  cat("Row AR1 parameter (rho_row):\n")
  cat("  Posterior mean:", round(mean(rho_row), 3), "\n")
  cat("  95% CrI:",
      round(quantile(rho_row, 0.025), 3), "-",
      round(quantile(rho_row, 0.975), 3), "\n")
}
```

**Interpretation:** A $\rho_r$ close to 1 indicates strong spatial
correlation along rows. Values above 0.3 generally justify the spatial
model. If $\rho_r \approx 0$, there is no spatial dependence in the row
direction, and the model reduces to iid residuals.


## Model 5b: AR1(row) x AR1(col) --- separable 2D spatial model

The standard ASReml spatial model uses a separable AR1 x AR1 structure:

```{r m5b-fit}
m_5b <- bayesreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ 1,
  random    = ~ gen,
  rcov      = ~ ar1(row):ar1(col),
  data      = serp,
  n_samples = 1000,
  warmup    = 500,
  chains    = 4
)

summary(m_5b)
```

### AR1 parameters for both dimensions

```{r m5b-ar1-params}
all_draws <- do.call(rbind, lapply(m_5b$greta$draws, as.matrix))
rho_cols <- grep("rho|ar1", colnames(all_draws), value = TRUE)

for (rc in rho_cols) {
  vals <- all_draws[, rc]
  cat(rc, ": mean =", round(mean(vals), 3),
      ", 95% CrI = [", round(quantile(vals, 0.025), 3), ",",
      round(quantile(vals, 0.975), 3), "]\n")
}
```

**Interpretation:** Typically $\rho_c$ (column autocorrelation) is
larger than $\rho_r$ (row autocorrelation) because plots within a column
share more soil characteristics. The product $\rho_r \cdot \rho_c$
gives the correlation between diagonally adjacent plots.


## Model 5c: IID row and column random effects

When AR1 is not appropriate, a simpler approach adds row and column as
IID random effects to absorb spatial gradients:

```{r m5c-fit}
m_5c <- bayesreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ 1,
  random    = ~ gen + row + col,
  data      = serp,
  n_samples = 1000,
  warmup    = 500,
  chains    = 4
)

summary(m_5c)
```

**Interpretation:** Adding row and column as IID random effects captures
broad spatial gradients without assuming a specific correlation decay.
This is a useful first step before committing to an AR1 model. If the
row/column variance components are large relative to the residual,
spatial trends are present and an AR1 model may further improve fit.


## Model 5d: AR1(row) with nested block effects

Another approach combines AR1 in one dimension with blocking in the
other. This is useful when columns form natural blocks (e.g., reps):

```{r m5d-fit}
m_5d <- bayesreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ 1,
  random    = ~ gen + col,
  rcov      = ~ ar1(row):id(col),
  data      = serp,
  n_samples = 1000,
  warmup    = 500,
  chains    = 4
)

summary(m_5d)
```

**Interpretation:** This model accounts for spatial autocorrelation
along rows via AR1, while column effects are absorbed by an IID random
term. This can be effective when the column direction shows discrete
jumps (e.g., between replicates) rather than smooth autocorrelation.


## Model comparison

```{r model-compare}
anova(m_base, m_5a, m_5b, m_5c, m_5d)
```

**Interpretation:** The AR1(row):AR1(col) model is the standard choice
for regular grid layouts (as used by ASReml). IID row/column effects
offer a simpler alternative when AR1 is not justified. The non-spatial
baseline should have the worst fit if spatial trends are present.


## Spatial residual diagnostics

### Residual heatmaps: before and after spatial correction

```{r residual-heatmaps, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
# Residuals from baseline (no spatial)
serp$resid_base <- residuals(m_base)

# Residuals from AR1xAR1 model
serp$resid_ar1  <- residuals(m_5b)

p_before <- ggplot(serp, aes(x = as.numeric(col), y = as.numeric(row),
                              fill = resid_base)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "grey90") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "Residual") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Row",
       title = "Residuals: no spatial model") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)) +
  coord_fixed()

p_after <- ggplot(serp, aes(x = as.numeric(col), y = as.numeric(row),
                             fill = resid_ar1)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "grey90") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "Residual") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Row",
       title = "Residuals: AR1(row) x AR1(col)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)) +
  coord_fixed()

p_before + p_after
```

**Interpretation:** The baseline residual map should show spatial
patterning (patches of similar colour). After spatial correction, the
residuals should appear more random, with no obvious patches or
gradients. If patterns remain, the spatial structure may need refinement
(e.g., adding row/column effects or using a more flexible model).


### Empirical variogram

```{r variogram, fig.width=6, fig.height=5}
# Compute empirical variogram from baseline residuals
resid_df <- serp %>%
  select(row_num, col_num, resid_base) %>%
  filter(!is.na(resid_base))

# Pairwise distances and squared differences
n <- nrow(resid_df)
pairs <- expand.grid(i = 1:n, j = 1:n) %>%
  filter(i < j)

pairs$dist <- sqrt(
  (resid_df$row_num[pairs$i] - resid_df$row_num[pairs$j])^2 +
  (resid_df$col_num[pairs$i] - resid_df$col_num[pairs$j])^2
)

pairs$semivar <- 0.5 * (resid_df$resid_base[pairs$i] -
                         resid_df$resid_base[pairs$j])^2

# Bin into distance classes
pairs$dist_class <- cut(pairs$dist,
                        breaks = seq(0, max(pairs$dist), length.out = 15))

vario <- pairs %>%
  group_by(dist_class) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_dist = mean(dist),
    semivariance = mean(semivar),
    n_pairs = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(dist_class))

ggplot(vario, aes(x = mean_dist, y = semivariance)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_pairs), colour = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "#D55E00",
              linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x     = "Distance (plot units)",
    y     = "Semivariance",
    size  = "N pairs",
    title = "Empirical variogram (baseline residuals)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
```

**Interpretation:** An increasing variogram (semivariance increases
with distance) confirms spatial autocorrelation. The distance at which
the variogram levels off (the "range") indicates the extent of spatial
dependence. If the variogram is flat from the origin, there is no
spatial correlation.


## Adjusted vs unadjusted BLUPs

A critical practical question: does the spatial model change genotype
rankings?

```{r blup-comparison, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
# BLUPs from baseline model
blups_base <- m_base$extras$blups$gen

# BLUPs from AR1xAR1 model
blups_ar1 <- m_5b$extras$blups$gen

# Match genotype names
common_gen <- intersect(names(blups_base), names(blups_ar1))

blup_compare <- data.frame(
  gen        = common_gen,
  unadjusted = blups_base[common_gen],
  adjusted   = blups_ar1[common_gen]
)

# Rank correlation
rank_cor <- cor(rank(blup_compare$unadjusted),
                rank(blup_compare$adjusted),
                method = "spearman")

ggplot(blup_compare, aes(x = unadjusted, y = adjusted)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#009E73", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x     = "BLUP (no spatial model)",
    y     = "BLUP (AR1 x AR1 spatial model)",
    title = paste0("BLUPs: spatial vs non-spatial (Spearman r = ",
                   round(rank_cor, 3), ")")
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
```

**Interpretation:** If the Spearman rank correlation is high (> 0.95),
the spatial model does not substantially alter genotype rankings, but
it still reduces standard errors (narrower CrIs). If rank correlation
is lower, spatial correction meaningfully changes which genotypes are
selected --- this justifies the additional model complexity.


### Top genotypes comparison

```{r top-genotypes}
blup_compare <- blup_compare %>%
  mutate(
    rank_unadj = rank(-unadjusted),
    rank_adj   = rank(-adjusted),
    rank_change = rank_unadj - rank_adj
  ) %>%
  arrange(rank_adj)

cat("Top 10 genotypes (spatially adjusted):\n")
print(head(blup_compare, 10))

cat("\nLargest rank changes:\n")
print(blup_compare %>% arrange(desc(abs(rank_change))) %>% head(5))
```


## Field map of adjusted BLUPs

```{r field-map, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
# Map BLUPs back to field positions
serp$blup_adj <- blups_ar1[as.character(serp$gen)]

ggplot(serp, aes(x = as.numeric(col), y = as.numeric(row),
                  fill = blup_adj)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "grey90") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#D55E00", mid = "white", high = "#009E73",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "BLUP") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(
    x     = "Column",
    y     = "Row",
    title = "Field map: spatially adjusted genotype BLUPs"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  coord_fixed()
```

```{r code-inspect}
# View the greta code generated for the AR1xAR1 model
cat(m_5b$extras$code)
```


## Tips for spatial models

1. **Regular vs irregular grids:** AR1 x AR1 is designed for regular
   rectangular grids where row and column indices are meaningful.
   For irregular layouts, use IID row/column random effects to absorb
   spatial variation without imposing a specific correlation structure.

2. **Serpentine harvesting:** The `gilmour.serpentine` dataset has a
   serpentine harvesting pattern. The AR1(col) parameter may capture
   harvester effects in addition to soil trends. Consider including
   explicit serpentine covariates if this is a concern.

3. **Row and column effects:** Before jumping to AR1, try adding row
   and column as fixed or random effects. Sometimes simple row/column
   adjustment is sufficient:
   ```r
   m_rowcol <- bayesreml(
     fixed  = yield ~ 1,
     random = ~ gen + row + col,
     data   = serp
   )
   ```

4. **Nugget effect:** The AR1 x AR1 model separates the variance into
   spatially correlated ($\sigma_\xi^2$) and independent
   ($\sigma_e^2$, the nugget) components. The ratio
   $\sigma_e^2 / (\sigma_\xi^2 + \sigma_e^2)$ indicates the proportion
   of non-spatial residual variation.

5. **Convergence:** Spatial autocorrelation parameters can be difficult
   to estimate. If convergence is poor (Rhat > 1.05), try:
   - Increasing `warmup` (e.g., 1000 or 2000)
   - Using a more informative `prior_vc_sd` (e.g., 0.5)
   - Simplifying to AR1 in one dimension only

6. **Anisotropy:** The separable AR1 x AR1 model naturally accommodates
   anisotropy (different correlation strengths in row vs column
   directions) through separate $\rho_r$ and $\rho_c$ parameters.

7. **Large fields:** For large fields (> 1000 plots), the dense
   correlation matrix can be computationally expensive. Consider
   sparse approximations or running on a GPU via
   `greta::install_greta_deps(type = "gpu")`.


## Summary

| Model    | Spatial structure                | Formula                             | Parameters |
|----------|----------------------------------|-------------------------------------|-----------|
| Baseline | None (iid)                       | `rcov = ~ units`                    | 1         |
| `m_5a`   | AR1 (rows only)                  | `rcov = ~ ar1(row):id(col)`        | 2         |
| `m_5b`   | AR1 x AR1 (2D)                   | `rcov = ~ ar1(row):ar1(col)`       | 3         |
| `m_5c`   | IID row + column random effects  | `random = ~ gen + row + col`        | 3         |
| `m_5d`   | AR1(row) + IID column random     | `rcov = ~ ar1(row):id(col)` + col   | 3         |

The AR1(row):AR1(col) model is the workhorse of spatial analysis in
plant breeding trials, directly equivalent to the standard ASReml
spatial model. The Bayesian implementation in `bayesreml` provides
full posterior distributions for all parameters including the
autocorrelation parameters, enabling proper uncertainty propagation
to genotype BLUPs and selection decisions.
